主要内容: The article discusses the perception of the U.S. stock market during the summer of 2013 as one of the most hated bull markets ever. Despite a 15% gain in the S&P 500 by early July, the rally was fueled by low-quality stocks with low price-to-earnings ratios, zero dividend yields, high short interest, and weak analyst ratings. Jeffrey D. Saut from Raymond James warned of a potential meaningful decline, citing the market's reliance on extreme monetary easing and the lack of confidence in the recovery. Bespoke Investment Group highlighted that the smallest stocks and those with the lowest P/E ratios outperformed, while high-dividend stocks lagged. Jim Paulsen from Wells Capital Management noted that the rally reflected a shift in confidence, with investors moving away from low-beta, high-dividend stocks toward higher-risk, higher-reward assets. The article suggests that the market's recovery was driven by a renewed sense of sustainability and confidence, even though it was marked by volatility and uncertainty.
